hook: Copper for the wires in your phone may have been dug in Chile, smelted beside the mine, shipped through a port, made into parts in China and sold by a store clerk near you, while engineers in California wrote its software. Every step is a different kind of work, done in a different place for a reason. Why is each step where it is?

prereq.q: What is the situation of a place?
options: Its location relative to other places, such as rivers, roads and markets
Its physical features, such as soil and climate
The feeling people have about it
prereq.why: Situation is a place's location relative to other places; factory location depends on it.

options: Lower cost per item when a firm produces in large amounts
Higher prices for goods made far away
Taxes on goods that cross a border
Small farms that sell at local markets
prereq.why: Producing more spreads fixed costs over more items, so each costs less.

figure.caption: The five economic sectors, from taking things from nature at the bottom to top decisions at the top.

chain.cause: A good is made from raw materials, by workers, for buyers
chain.effect: its maker weighs the costs of raw materials, labor, energy and transport

chain.cause: A product weighs less than its raw materials (weight-losing)
chain.effect: the factory locates near the raw materials, as copper smelters do near Chile's mines

chain.cause: A product weighs more than its inputs (weight-gaining)
chain.effect: the factory locates near its market, as soft-drink bottlers do near cities

chain.cause: Goods switch from ships to trains at a port (a break-of-bulk point)
chain.effect: processing plants cluster there, as at Rotterdam

ideas: Five sectors: primary (take from nature), secondary (make goods), tertiary (services), quaternary (information and research), quinary (top decisions).
Sort a job by what the worker does, not by what the firm sells.
Least cost theory: a factory locates where transport, labor and nearby-firm costs are lowest. Weight-losing industries go to the raw material; weight-gaining ones go to the market.
A break-of-bulk point is where goods change transport modes, such as a port; processing clusters there.
Countries often classed as core have mostly service, research and decision jobs; those often classed as periphery have more primary work; the semiperiphery is in between.

misconception.wrong: A factory always locates where wages are lowest.
misconception.right: Labor is one cost among several. A copper smelter sits by the mine to avoid hauling waste rock, a bottler sits by its buyers, and Iceland's aluminum smelters follow cheap power. The heaviest cost decides.

summary: Jobs fall into five sectors, from taking resources from nature to making the top decisions. Factories locate to keep total costs low: weight-losing industries near raw materials, weight-gaining ones near markets, and processing at break-of-bulk points. Core countries have mostly service and research jobs; the periphery more primary work.
